h1:
Isan Food in Korat
10 Spots Locals Actually Eat At
intro: Korat is the gateway to Isan, and the som tum and grilled chicken here are more serious than you'd expect, because the city has its own Korat-style som tum — a middle ground between Thai-style and fermented-fish (pla ra) style, made with ground dried fish and ginger, so it lands sour, spicy and salty with a touch of sweetness behind it. We picked the places Korat people genuinely sit down to eat at, from Michelin Bib Gourmand restaurants to a market stall that's been going for 30 years.

blocks.html: Before we run through the restaurants, here's why Isan food in Korat isn't quite like anywhere else. Korat people speak the Korat dialect (not full Lao-Isan), so the food sits right in the middle. Korat-style som tum gets its savory depth from ground dried fish and fermented field crab rather than going heavy on pla ra like Lao-style tum, but it isn't sweet-forward like central Thai-style tum either. It pairs with larb, nam tok, grilled pork neck, and the rotisserie grilled chicken the city is known for. This list runs from the most talked-about spots down, and every one is open and worth eating at right now.

blocks.text: 10 Isan Restaurants in Korat Locals Go To

items.name: Larb Somphit (Trok Chan)
items.blurb: A legendary spot in the middle of town, open for over 50 years and a Michelin Bib Gourmand pick several years running. Known for cooked-beef larb, sweet liver and grilled tongue in a punchy, old-school style. Busy from mid-morning, and some dishes sell out before closing.
items.meta: Trok Chan area, in town · open 07:00–16:00 daily

items.name: Gai Yang Saeng Thai
items.blurb: Korat's long-running rotisserie grilled chicken shop, on Ratchadamnoen Road near the Thao Suranari (Ya Mo) monument, and a Bib Gourmand pick too. They do both farmed and free-range chicken with a house marinade — fragrant skin, juicy meat, ready to eat alongside som tum.
items.meta: Ratchadamnoen Road, near the Ya Mo monument · before the IT junction

items.name: Som Tum Pa Nang (Night Suan Mak)
items.blurb: A som tum stall in the market that's been going for over 30 years, on Manat Road opposite the BAAC bank. The standouts are the crab-and-pla-ra tum and the savory Korat-style tum, with fragrant fermented fish and easy prices. Open late, so it's good for dinner.
items.meta: Manat Road, in town (Night Suan Mak) · open late morning–22:00

items.name: Tom Saep Kaen Khon (Suep Siri)
items.blurb: An open-air spot with wooden tables in Soi Suep Siri. Locals like it because the food comes fast, the service is good and the prices are friendly. Som tum, tom saep and punchy larb — a good place to settle in for the evening.
items.meta: Soi Suep Siri, in town · open-air

items.name: Som Tum Phan Lan (Zoo Entrance)
items.blurb: A legendary som tum stall right by the entrance to Korat Zoo. They shred the papaya by hand, serve fast and have plenty of unusual dishes to try. The Korat-style tum is properly spicy — a handy stop on the way to the zoo.
items.meta: By Korat Zoo entrance · several branches

items.name: Som Tum Phi At
items.blurb: A heavily reviewed som tum spot in town, known for fiery tum served on a big tray. If you love it really spicy, this is the one. Order it with grilled chicken and sticky rice for a full meal.

items.name: Som Tum Warakon
items.blurb: A trackside spot people know for its cockle and seafood tum. Fresh ingredients, bold flavors — better for fans of seafood tum than for the traditional pla-ra style.

items.name: Som Tum Ngan Taeng
items.blurb: A small shop in the shade of the trees that locals love for its tum with crispy noodles and pla-ra sauce — homey and savory, with an easy-going feel, light prices, and good for an afternoon snack.

items.name: Som Tum Amnuay
items.blurb: An old street stall that Korat people think of fondly — the same hand for years, simple tum done just right, cheap prices. A good quick stop while you're walking around town.

items.name: Baan Paeng Hom
items.blurb: Not a som tum-only place but a Thai–Korat restaurant with a Bib Gourmand, open for over 20 years. The standouts are the crab-and-pla-ra tum and Korat-style pad mee. Good for a relaxed, air-conditioned sit-down meal.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Old-school spots like Larb Somphit and Gai Yang Saeng Thai sell out fast — go before noon to get the full menu. Market stalls like Pa Nang, on the other hand, come alive in the evening.

blocks.text: How Korat-style som tum differs from Lao and Thai styles

blocks.html: If you come all the way to Korat and only order Thai-style tum, you'll miss the city's signature. Korat-style som tum sits right in the middle: it's made with ground dried fish (smoked, sun-dried fish ground to a powder), ginger, and either boiled pla-ra sauce or fermented field crab. The flavor is sour, spicy and salty with a little sweetness behind it — unlike Lao-style tum, which isn't sweet and leans harder on pla ra, and unlike Thai-style tum, which is sweet-forward. Many Korat shops serve a Korat tray with the tum alongside fermented rice noodles, vegetables and grilled chicken.

items: Korat-style tum — a hybrid of Thai and pla-ra styles, with ground dried fish and ginger, savory and well-rounded
Lao-style tum — heavy on pla-ra sauce, bold and unsweetened, properly spicy
Tum sua — fermented rice noodles or thin noodles pounded into the mortar, more filling than plain tum
Crab-and-pla-ra tum — made with fermented field crab and pla ra, the version locals order most

blocks.text: Larb, nam tok, grilled pork neck — what to order

blocks.html: Good Isan food isn't only about tum — larb and nam tok are the other stars. Larb is minced beef or pork tossed with roasted rice powder and larb seasoning, while nam tok uses the same dressing but with sliced grilled meat instead of mince. At Larb Somphit, try the cooked-beef larb, sweet liver and grilled tongue. At a regular Isan place, order grilled pork neck with jaew dipping sauce to go with sticky rice and you can't go wrong.

items.name: Beef larb / nam tok
items.blurb: Tossed with fragrant roasted rice powder, sour and spicy, eaten with fresh veg and sticky rice. Order it cooked if you're not into raw.

items.name: Grilled pork neck + jaew
items.blurb: Grilled tender, not chewy, dipped in punchy jaew sauce — the go-to side at every Isan shop.

items.name: Tom saep
items.blurb: Sipped hot, sour and spicy, it cuts the richness — good to order between the tum and the grilled meats.

blocks.text: How to pick the right spot for you

blocks.html: Want Michelin-guide-level old-school food? Hit Larb Somphit or Gai Yang Saeng Thai in the late morning. Want to settle in open-air for the evening? Go to Tom Saep Kaen Khon or Pa Nang in the market. If you're walking around town and want something quick, street stalls like Som Tum Amnuay or Ngan Taeng are fast and cheap. To be straight with you, some of the famous spots have long queues at peak times and are genuinely spicy — if you don't handle heat well, order it mild to start.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Many of the old-school spots are mostly cash-only and have little parking. If you're heading to a place in town during peak hours, it's easier to park further out and walk in.

faq.q: How is Korat-style som tum different from regular som tum?
faq.a: Korat-style som tum is a hybrid between Thai-style and pla-ra-style tum, made with ground dried fish and ginger. It comes out sour, spicy and salty with a touch of sweetness behind it — not as heavy on pla ra as Lao-style tum, and not as sweet-forward as Thai-style tum. Many shops serve it as a Korat tray alongside fermented rice noodles and vegetables.

faq.q: Which Isan restaurants in Korat have a Michelin Guide listing?
faq.a: Larb Somphit at Trok Chan and Gai Yang Saeng Thai on Ratchadamnoen Road both hold Bib Gourmand awards from the Michelin Guide, along with Baan Paeng Hom, known for its crab-and-pla-ra tum and Korat-style pad mee.

faq.q: Where should I go for rotisserie grilled chicken in Korat?
faq.a: Gai Yang Saeng Thai on Ratchadamnoen Road near the Ya Mo monument is the long-running shop people think of first. They do both farmed and free-range chicken at around 150 THB per bird, ready to eat with som tum. It sells out fast, so go before noon.

faq.q: Are there som tum spots in Korat that stay open late?
faq.a: Yes. Som Tum Pa Nang in the Night Suan Mak market on Manat Road stays open until around 22:00, and Tom Saep Kaen Khon in Soi Suep Siri is a good place to settle in for the evening. Both work well for dinner.

faq.q: Roughly how much does an Isan meal in Korat cost per person?
faq.a: Som tum runs about 40–80 THB a plate, larb or grilled pork neck about 60–120 THB a plate, and grilled chicken around 150 THB a bird. With two or three people ordering a full spread it works out to roughly 100–250 THB a head. Street stalls come in cheaper than that.
